name: Glycolic acid peel
lead: A glycolic acid peel is a superficial chemical peel using glycolic acid, an alpha-hydroxy acid. Alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) are described by Wikipedia as the mildest peels, used for fine wrinkles, dryness, uneven pigment and acne [11]. One article calls it one of the most versatile agents in melasma treatment [2].

Studies in Indian and other patient groups have examined glycolic peels, at concentrations such as 20% or 30%, for melasma, periorbital melanosis and acne scars, often alone against other peels or combined with other agents [1][2][3][4].
infobox: Melasma, periorbital melanosis, acne scars, photoaging [1][2][3][8]

paras: A 2011 study combined microneedling with glycolic acid peels for acne scars in dark skin, noting that acne scars often coexist with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation [1]. A 2017 study examined a glycolic peel combined with 20% azelaic acid cream in melasma, assessing efficacy, safety and quality of life [2].

A comparative study of 90 patients with periorbital melanosis tested 20% glycolic peels, 15% lactic peels and 20% vitamin C [3], and a later study added a 12% ferulic acid peel [4]. Registered trials include glycolic acid against salicylic acid for melasma [5][6], 70% glycolic acid with vitamin C for photoaging and acne scars [7][8], and a comparison against a 1064 nm Q-switched laser for melasma [9]. A 2025 systematic review of randomized trials covered topical treatments for acanthosis nigricans [10].

Wikipedia notes that complications rise with peel depth and can include prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia and skin thinning, and that light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness. Wikipedia adds that low-strength home kits can cause injury and scarring [11].

card.summary: The most widely studied AHA peel, tested in melasma, periorbital darkening and acne scars in mostly small studies.
card.note: Stinging, redness and dryness are common; home kits have been associated with injury.

quick.overview:
A glycolic acid peel exfoliates the skin using an alpha-hydroxy acid and is used for pigmentation, acne scars and general texture.

It has the largest body of small comparative studies among the common peels, though many are from single centers.
quick.mechanism: It is a mild superficial peel that loosens the outer skin layers, which then shed.
quick.risks: Common effects are stinging, redness, irritation and dryness; pigment change is among reported complications, and Wikipedia notes weak home kits can cause injury and scarring.
